odor: Odorless (natural gas odor is added mercaptans)
environmentalPersistence: Moderate as atmospheric gas — atmospheric half-life ~12 years; 86× more potent GHG than CO₂ over 20 years

lowDose.description: No direct plant effects at background concentrations. Recent research shows low-dose methane may function as a signaling molecule — promoting seed germination, lateral root growth, and mild stress tolerance. Emerging science.

highDose.description: Soil methane from anaerobic decomposition displaces O₂ in rhizosphere — root hypoxia, aerenchyma formation, reduced aerobic respiration. Also soil methane oxidizing bacteria outcompete PGPR.

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Moderate at high dose — root hypoxia from O₂ displacement reduces water/nutrient uptake
morphologicalEffects.wilting: Moderate — root dysfunction impairs water uptake
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Moderate — hypoxia-induced chloroplast stress and nutrient deficiency from impaired roots
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Mild to moderate — root tip necrosis from anaerobic conditions
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Modified — aerenchyma formation (air channels) as adaptive response; but overall root function reduced
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Old leaves show chlorosis from chronic nutrient stress; wilting appears across canopy

physiologyEffects.waterUptake: Impaired — root hypoxia reduces water conductance
physiologyEffects.nutrientTransport: Disrupted — anaerobic root conditions prevent normal nutrient uptake

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Moderate — hypoxia followed by re-oxygenation generates ROS

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Strong — methane soil environment selects for methanotrophs and anaerobes at expense of aerobic diversity
microbiomeEffects.beneficialBacteriaEffect: Strongly suppressed — aerobic PGPR displaced by anaerobic community
microbiomeEffects.fungalEffect: Anaerobic conditions suppress most beneficial fungi; some pathogenic anaerobic fungi may increase
microbiomeEffects.rhizosphereStability: Strongly altered — complete aerobic-to-anaerobic community shift

temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: 1–3 weeks if methane source removed and soil re-oxygenated
temporalDynamics.sensitization: Aerenchyma formation is adaptive — acclimated plants develop better flood/hypoxia tolerance

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Green → wilted → mild chlorosis; aerenchyma formation visible in root cross-sections
visualSimulation.firstAffectedRegion: Root zone first; wilting propagates upward
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Flooding/waterlogging visual — diagnostic for anaerobic root stress
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate — ethanol and lactate fermentation metabolite signature; distinctive anaerobic profile
visualSimulation.microbiomeParticles: Community shift visible — aerobic particles disappear; anaerobic methanotroph cluster forms
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Moderate — aerenchyma tissue persists; new root growth resumes after re-oxygenation

synergies.synergyNote: Methane and CO₂ are both products of anaerobic decomposition in wetlands and landfills — co-occurrence is realistic. Both accumulate in soil gas phase under waterlogged conditions.
synergies.antagonismNote: Atmospheric methane is oxidized by OH radicals that also destroy ozone — indirect interaction affecting ozone chemistry

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Wetlands (largest natural source), livestock digestion and manure, landfills, rice paddies, natural gas leaks, permafrost thaw
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Not applied intentionally; produced by rice paddy agriculture and livestock — major agricultural GHG
educationalContext.humanToxicity: Not toxic at atmospheric concentrations; simple asphyxiant at very high concentrations; highly flammable
educationalContext.climateLink: Second most important anthropogenic greenhouse gas after CO₂; 86× more potent over 20 years. Permafrost thaw releasing methane stored for millennia is a key climate feedback. Livestock methane is ~14.5% of global GHG emissions.
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Outdoor — atmospheric; soil gas near landfills and wetlands; indoor leak hazard
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: Cow burps and farts — livestock are one of the largest methane sources. Landfills in every community emit methane. Permafrost methane release is one of the most feared climate tipping points.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Livestock agriculture emissions, landfill gas, permafrost tipping points, rice paddy emissions
